title: Clustering: finding natural groups
hook: Hand rules, k-means, hierarchical, density-based and mixtures. Group customers with no labels.
inPlainWords: Clustering sorts alike items into groups when nobody has said what the groups are. You choose the method, the number of groups, and which features count as "alike".

useCase.title: Group 50,000 customers for different emails
useCase.story: ShopEase wants customer segments for marketing. Nobody has labeled them. The columns are spend, visit frequency, product mix, discount use and days since last visit.

approaches.name: Hand-made buckets
approaches.what: Split by simple thresholds, like big spenders and frequent visitors.
approaches.greatWhen: You want something quick and explainable, with no ML.
approaches.avoidWhen: Patterns are subtle and the thresholds are arbitrary.
approaches.example: Spend over $500 and five or more visits is a VIP.

approaches.name: K-means
approaches.what: You pick the number of groups. The method finds a center for each and assigns every customer to the nearest.
approaches.greatWhen: A fast baseline for roundish, similar-sized groups.
approaches.avoidWhen: Odd-shaped groups or lots of outliers.

approaches.name: Hierarchical clustering
approaches.what: Merges the most alike customers step by step into a tree of groups.
approaches.greatWhen: You want to see groups at several levels, with modest data.
approaches.example: Gift buyers split into corporate gifts and personal gifts.

approaches.name: Density-based clustering
approaches.what: Finds crowded regions and treats lonely points as noise.
approaches.example: A tight cluster of night-time shoppers, plus scattered oddballs.

approaches.name: Overlapping groups (mixtures)
approaches.what: Gives every customer a probability of belonging to each group.
approaches.greatWhen: Customers really belong to several segments.
approaches.example: A customer is 70% bargain hunter and 30% gift buyer.

approaches.name: Embed first, then cluster
approaches.what: Turn text or images into embeddings, then cluster those.
approaches.avoidWhen: Tabular data that is already numeric.

challenge.question: You need segments marketing can act on, from 50,000 customers with no labels. What is the smart approach?

options.text: Cluster on well-chosen, scaled features, compare a few group counts, then name and test the groups
options.why: It produces groups people understand, and the test tells you whether they matter.

options.text: Ask for 50 groups so each is very specific
options.why: Marketing cannot run 50 campaigns, and small groups are mostly noise.
Clusters need a human check. They can be meaningless.
Explainable and quick, but you may miss real patterns.

bestCase.title: Pick sensible features, try a few group counts, then name the groups
bestCase.example: K-means with five groups finds bargain hunters, gift buyers, loyal regulars, new browsers and lapsed customers. Marketing reads a sample from each, names them, and sends different emails. A later test shows which email works for which group.

worstCase.title: Clustering on unscaled data and trusting the output
worstCase.example: Spend is in dollars and visits are small counts, so spend dominates. The "clusters" are just spending bands. Marketing launches five campaigns that are really the same campaign with different discounts.

steps.label: Raw customer data
steps.goes: Spend, visits, product mix, days since the last visit.

steps.label: Choose and scale features
steps.goes: Put the numbers on similar scales.
steps.goesWrong: Raw numbers go in as they are. Dollars drown out everything else.

steps.label: Look at each group
steps.goes: Read a sample of real customers from each group.

steps.label: Name the groups
steps.goes: Bargain hunters, gift buyers, loyal regulars and so on.

steps.label: Test with campaigns
steps.goes: See which message works for which group.

takeaway: Clustering only finds groups. People decide whether the groups are meaningful and useful.
